blocks.text: We have seen that linear momentum plays an important role in the translational motion of bodies; similarly, another quantity known as angular momentum has an important role in the study of rotational motion.

blocks.title: Angular momentum
blocks.text: A particle is said to possess an angular momentum about a reference axis if it so moves that its angular position changes relative to that reference axis. The angular momentum L of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v and momentum p (Fig. 3.16, as printed) relative to the origin O is defined as L = r x p ... (3.20), where r is the position vector of the particle at that instant relative to O. Angular momentum is a vector quantity; its magnitude is L = r p sin theta = m r v sin theta, where theta is the angle between r and p. The direction of L is perpendicular to the plane formed by r and p, with its sense given by the right-hand rule of the vector product. The SI unit of angular momentum is kg m^2 s^-1 or J s.

If the particle moves in a circle of radius r with uniform angular velocity omega, the angle between r and the tangential velocity is 90 degrees; hence L = m r v sin 90 = m r v, and as v = r omega, L = m r^2 omega. Now consider a symmetric rigid body rotating about a fixed axis through its centre of mass (Fig. 3.17). Each particle of the body rotates about the same axis in a circle with angular velocity omega. The magnitude of the angular momentum of the particle of mass m_i is m_i v_i r_i about the origin O, and the direction of L_i is the same as that of omega. Since v_i = r_i omega, the angular momentum of the i-th particle is m_i r_i^2 omega; summing over all particles gives the total angular momentum of the rigid body, L = (sum of m_i r_i^2) omega = I omega, where I is the moment of inertia of the rigid body about the axis of rotation. A sphere rotating in the sense of the gold arrow has its angular velocity and angular momentum taken upward along the rotational axis, as the right-hand rule shows (For Your Information).

blocks.title: Example 3.5
blocks.text: The mass of the Earth is 6.00 x 10^24 kg and the distance r from the Earth to the Sun is 1.50 x 10^11 m. As seen from the direction of the North Star the Earth revolves counter-clockwise around the Sun. Determine the orbital angular momentum of the Earth about the Sun, assuming it traverses a circular orbit once a year (3.16 x 10^7 s). Solution: to find the orbital angular momentum we first need the orbital speed. Moving around a circle of radius r, the Earth travels a distance 2 pi r in one year, so its orbital speed is v_o = 2 pi r / t. Orbital angular momentum of the Earth = L_o = m v_o r = 2 pi r^2 m / t = 2 pi (1.50 x 10^11 m)^2 (6.00 x 10^24 kg) / (3.16 x 10^7 s) = 2.67 x 10^40 kg m^2 s^-1. The sign is positive because the revolution is counter-clockwise.

blocks.caption: Moment of inertia, angular momentum and its conservation (original diagram after Figures 3.15 to 3.23 and topics 3.4 to 3.6).
blocks.long_description: A force at right angles to a rod gives the mass at its end a tangential acceleration, and multiplying by the radius turns the law of motion into torque equals mass times radius squared times angular acceleration, so the mass times the square of its distance from the axis plays the part of mass; for a rigid body the sum of these over all its pieces is the moment of inertia, largest when mass sits far from the axis. The angular momentum of a particle is the vector product of its position vector and its momentum, perpendicular to their plane by the right-hand rule, equal to mass times radius times speed for circular motion and to the moment of inertia times the angular velocity for a rigid body. With no external torque the total angular momentum of a system is constant, so when a diver or skater draws the limbs in the moment of inertia falls and the spin speeds up, a flywheel stores rotational energy and steadies machines, and a fast-spinning gyroscope holds its axis in space and guides aircraft, submarines and spacecraft.

blocks.prompt: A bicycle wheel has angular momentum 10 kg m^2 s^-1 and angular velocity 2 rad s^-1; find its moment of inertia (numerical problem 3.9). Show that for orbital motion L = I omega (comprehensive question 3.2).
blocks.explanation: I = L / omega = 10 / 2 = 5 kg m^2. For a particle in a circle L = m r v with v = r omega, so L = m r^2 omega; since the moment of inertia of a point mass about the axis is I = m r^2, L = I omega, the same form as for a rigid body.

items: L = r x p; magnitude r p sin theta = m r v sin theta; direction perpendicular to r and p by the right-hand rule; unit kg m^2 s^-1 = J s.
Circle: L = m r v = m r^2 omega. Rigid body: L = I omega along the axis. Example 3.5: Earth's orbital angular momentum 2.67 x 10^40 kg m^2 s^-1, positive (counter-clockwise).
